edits.old: Under the bounded-mass hypotheses of \cref{chap:envelopes}, upper and lower volumes supply invariants of ordinary singularity type. For the general theory, the relative envelope condition and the finite damped measures are already available without those hypotheses. Finiteness and continuity of the undamped measure require their own estimates, which can be imposed on the sequence used in a proof. Multiplier-ideal equivalence is coarser than bounded equivalence and is not built into these definitions. The next comparison with $\mathcal I$-goodness must determine which volume and envelope identities survive that coarser relation.

edits.old:
Set $f_j=\max(f,-j)$ and $p_j=P_\theta(f_j)$. These envelopes are genuine because $p$ is a competitor. They have a common finite upper bound. Here is the elementary reason: $f_1$ is finite almost everywhere, so some set $A=\{f_1\leq N\}$ has positive smooth volume. For any competitor $a\leq f_1$ quasi-everywhere, the uniform $L^1$ bound for $a-\sup_Xa$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{Vol}(A)(\sup_Xa-N)
       \leq\int_A(\sup_Xa-a)\,\mathrm{d}V\leq C.
\]
The same bound applies to its envelope, and hence to all $p_j$. Choose $M$ strictly larger than this common upper bound.
edits.new: Set $f_j=\max(f,-j)$ and $p_j=P_\theta(f_j)$. The genuine potential $p$ is a competitor for every obstacle. Since $f_j\leq f_1$ and $f_1$ is finite almost everywhere, the finite-sublevel argument at the start of \cref{chap:envelopes} gives a common upper bound for all competitors. Thus the envelopes $p_j$ are genuine and uniformly bounded above. Choose $M$ strictly larger than this bound.
